items.abstract: <jats:p>Shareholder voting rights are indispensable to the functioning of the shareholders' meeting and to the protection of shareholder interests. Through voting, shareholders transform individual preferences into legally cognizable expressions of will, which, under capital-majority rule, may become the will of the company. This article analyzes the meaning and legal nature of shareholder voting rights; the one-shareone-vote principle and its exceptions; the personal, proxy, and written exercise of voting rights; proxy solicitation; split voting; voting agreements; and exclusion of interested shareholders from voting. The article characterizes voting rights as inherent, common-benefit, individual shareholder rights and as a special form of civil right. It argues that cumulative voting is not an exception to one-share-one-vote; that non-voting preferred shares should be permitted, with voting rights reviving when promised preferential dividends are not paid; that multiple-vote shares may be exceptionally authorized in special circumstances; that treasury shares and cross-held shares should not carry exercisable voting rights; and that proxy solicitation requires strict legal regulation. It further supports written voting as a means of allowing absent shareholders to express their own will directly, generally rejects split voting absent special justification, recognizes the validity of shareholder voting agreements that do not violate mandatory law, public order, good morals, or the prohibition on abuse of rights, and advocates an interested-shareholder voting-exclusion regime to restrain abuse of capital-majority rule.</jats:p>
title: On Shareholders' Voting Rights

items.abstract: <jats:p>One of the cornerstones of takeover regulation is the required bid rule (MBR), which requires an acquirer who gains "control" over a target firm to make an offer to buy the shares of the remaining owners. It is not entirely clear what constitutes "control," as some jurisdictions take a quantitative approach based on a specific shareholding threshold, such as 30% voting rights, while others take a qualitative approach based on a subjective assessment based on a number of factors, such as the specific rights that an acquirer would have under a shareholders' agreement or the target's governing documents.<br><br>This paper analyses the combined approach undertaken by the Indian takeover code and attempts to examine Veto rights under their ambit. And how even till date, veto rights as an aspect of ‘control’ remains a subjective test.</jats:p>
title: Veto Rights and Concept of Corporate 'Control'

items.abstract: <jats:p>After examining the concept and historical evolution of cumulative voting, this article argues that China's Company Law should establish a mandatory cumulative-voting regime for the election of directors and supervisors. It revisits the major arguments advanced by U.S. scholars for and against cumulative voting and contends that the mechanism can improve the effectiveness of corporate governance, advance shareholder equality and shareholder democracy, and protect minority shareholders. To enhance transparency and fairness, the article proposes procedural prerequisites for exercising cumulative voting rights, recommends the joint election of directors and supervisors, and argues that an election remains valid even when minority shareholders, through a superior voting strategy, elect a majority of the available seats. It also explains methods for calculating the minimum number of shares needed to elect a specified number of directors and the number of directors that can be elected with a fixed block of shares. Finally, it evaluates devices used to restrict or dilute cumulative voting, including classified boards, reductions in board size, obstruction of minorityelected directors, and removal without cause.</jats:p>
title: On Shareholders' Cumulative Voting Rights

<jats:p><p><span>The Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD) distinguishes between crisis prevention and crisis management measures. The former, including early intervention measures, are the responsibility of the supervisory authority, while resolution is the responsibility of the resolution authority. In outlining this distinction, the BRRD also clarifies the scope within which early intervention measures can affect shareholders' rights. It is made clear that such tools cannot dissolve corporate bodies and suspend the functioning of the shareholders' meeting. Such effects are typical of resolution as a crisis management measure. </span></p>
<p><span>The European Central Bank is now the competent authority for applying early intervention measures to significant banks. In this context, it is responsible for enforcing relevant EU and national legislation. However, Member States' legislation may differ from European law. One example is the Italian extraordinary administration. This procedure, which falls somewhere between early intervention measures and administrative compulsory liquidation, differs in many respects from the provisions of Article 29, BRRD. This led to a dispute over the annulment of the extraordinary administration measure adopted by the European Central Bank with regard to Banca Carige.</span></p>
<p><span>Against this backdrop, the paper aims to verify the compatibility of Italian legislation with European laws. It concludes that domestic law has not complied with the BRRD insofar as it has regulated a procedure that corresponds to a crisis management tool as a preventive measure. The paper also analyses the relationship between EU law and non-compliant national law, concluding that the former takes precedence in the event of a conflict.</span></p></jats:p>
title: Early Intervention Measures and Shareholders' Rights
